query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Coupled Thermodynamic–Kinetic Modeling Accurately Predicts Phase Transformation Boundaries
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy prepared as a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase
generation.intervention: Utilize a predictive simulation framework (CALPHAD integrated with kinetic Monte Carlo) to design thermal processing routes
generation.conditions: Apply simulation at temperatures ranging from 1200 °C down to 600 °C and then experimentally validate with controlled cooling experiments in an inert atmosphere
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of short-range order parameters and corresponding free-energy landscapes that demarcate the transition from disordered BCC to ordered (B2-like) states
generation.mechanism: This hypothesis contends that the phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is determined by a combined effect: a composition-dependent thermodynamic instability (captured via CALPHAD free-energy curves) and kinetic limitations (simulated via kMC modeling of atomic diffusion). The interplay of these factors predicts a distinct transformation temperature that separates the high-temperature BCC state from the low-temperature ordered state.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict a transformation onset temperature within a ±50 °C window; experimental cooling treatments should reveal an inflection in phase fraction near this predicted temperature, with marked differences between samples cooled above and below this threshold.
generation.baseline: Standard processing based solely on equilibrium thermodynamics without kinetic considerations, which does not accurately capture the observed phase transformation behavior
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies as long as the alloy remains compositionally homogeneous and free of external mechanical perturbations that might bias diffusion paths.
generation.uncertainty: Potential inaccuracies in the thermodynamic databases or kMC parameters may introduce uncertainty in the predicted transformation temperature and phase boundaries.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform simulations using the coupled modeling approach to extract a predicted transformation temperature, then conduct a series of cooling experiments with precise thermal control and measure phase fractions via XRD and TEM.
measurements: Simulated transformation temperature from the model
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally observed transformation temperature deviates by more than the stated uncertainty (e.g., > ±50 °C) from the model prediction, or if the kinetic pathway does not match model predictions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Below, we present both calculations and experiments that are consistent with these main transformations in AlxCoCrFeNi, for 1 < x < 2: on cooling from high temperatures (near melting), the high-temperature BCC solid solution transforms into a partially ordered B2 phase. Upon further cooling, the partially ordered B2 phase transforms into a phase mixture comprised of disordered BCC (primarily Co and Fe) plus a B2 phase (primarily composed of Ni-Co-Al). This two-step transformation is illustrated using Monte Carlo simulations (Fig. 1).

cited_evidence.kind: web:Monte Carlo model for multi-component transformations
cited_evidence.text: The values of vij are given in Table 1, for the simulations presented, as well as some related components. These values are reasonable, in light of prior experimental observations. First, the interactions between Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni are all small (magnitudes < 2 kJ/mol), indicating the weak interactions in the single-phase forming “Cantor” alloy of CrCrFeMnNi. Second, the addition of Al shows a favorable interaction with every other component, with particular strong interactions with Ni and Co. This trend immediately suggests the formation of a Ni-Co-Al phase at low temperatures, as has been observed,,. Roughly speaking, the Co and Ni interactions are reasonably similar, and our results presented below demonstrate that Co and Ni have similar behaviors. Finally, we note that with the exception of weakly attractive interactions with Ni and Al, Cu has a positive interaction with all other components. Thus, we may expect that Cu will tend to segregate away from the others. This trend has been observed experimentally, and is supported by simulations,,,.

papers.title: Atomistic clustering‐ordering and high‐strain deformation of an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high‐entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Force-field development validated against first‐principles and MD simulations to study atomic pair correlations and clustering behavior
papers.findings: Electronic-structure–based linear-response calculations and MD simulations identify strong Al–Ni pair correlations that drive clustering (particularly Al–Al clustering) even with temperature elevation, with evidence for a clustering-to-ordering transition under compressive loading.
papers.mechanism: Phase stability is governed by localized pair interactions (especially Al–Ni correlations) that promote clustering, which can evolve into ordering under high strain; these atomic-scale correlations indicate an interplay between thermodynamic instability (spinodal decomposition-like behavior) and kinetic response under load.

papers.title: Predictive multiphase evolution in Al‐containing high‐entropy alloys.
papers.system: AlxCoCrFeNi alloys, with focus on compositions where Al strengthens the multiphase microstructure
papers.approach: High-throughput Monte Carlo simulations parameterized via first‐principles inputs complemented by neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry to study temperature-dependent ordering phenomena
papers.findings: Simulations reproduce the key features of Al-induced ordering within a high-temperature BCC phase, predicting a B2 ordering temperature that scales with Al content. A two-step transformation is shown: initially a BCC solid solution partially orders into a Ni–Co–Al-rich B2 phase, and further cooling induces phase separation into a mixture of ordered and disordered BCC phases.
papers.mechanism: The transformation is interpreted as a competition between thermodynamic driving forces (via favorable pair interactions such as those between Al, Co, and Ni leading to B2 order) and kinetic effects (evidenced by diffusionless ordering at high temperature and kinetic arrest under rapid cooling), thereby governing phase selection.

papers.title: Orientation Relationships in Al0.7CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Experimental microstructural characterization via EBSD/TEM to establish orientation relationships and compositional partitioning between phases
papers.findings: Reveals a Widmanstätten microstructure where a high-temperature BCC parent phase, enriched in Al and Cr, gives rise to an FCC daughter phase with complementary composition; the transformation exhibits a characteristic diffusionless pattern and distinct crystallographic orientation relationships.
papers.mechanism: Suggests that phase stability and transformation are governed by diffusionless martensitic-type transitions controlled mainly by crystallographic symmetry changes and compositional partitioning that minimize interfacial energy under fast cooling conditions.

papers.title: The Observation of Cellular Precipitation in an Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 High-Entropy Alloy after Qu
papers.system: Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 HEA, comparable to Cr–Co–Fe–Ni–Al systems
papers.approach: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to analyze lamellar precipitation patterns after quenching and isothermal holding
papers.findings: Documented the formation of cellular precipitation featuring lamellar L12 particles rich in Ni and Al coexisting with a re-precipitated FCC matrix; elemental line scans indicate marked segregation that defines the distinct phases.
papers.mechanism: Cellular precipitation is driven by compositional supersaturation and diffusion-mediated partitioning at grain boundaries, showcasing a kinetic pathway that competes with and eventually overcomes the high-temperature BCC state, providing insight into how thermodynamic instability is relieved through phase separation.

established: Phase selection in Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys is strongly affected by both composition (especially Al, Co, Ni content) and thermal history.
High-temperature BCC states in these multicomponent alloys can undergo ordering (e.g., B2 formation) or phase separation as temperature decreases.
Both atomistic pair interactions (notably Al–Ni and Al–Co) and kinetic factors (e.g., cooling rate, strain-induced effects) are critical in dictating phase evolution.

approaches_tried.approach: Atomistic simulations (MD with validated force-fields, Monte Carlo methods)
approaches_tried.outcome: Effectively captured short-range ordering, clustering, and predicted B2 ordering temperatures; however, direct prediction of phase boundaries across thermal regimes remains challenging.
Resolved phase morphology, orientation relationships, and compositional segregation; provided evidence for diffusionless transformations and cellular precipitation.

approaches_tried.approach: Calorimetry and thermodynamic modeling (CALPHAD, first-principles-based Monte Carlo)
approaches_tried.outcome: Mapped temperature-composition phase boundaries and connected predicted ordering temperatures with experimental observations, though coupling of kinetic behavior remains partially unresolved.

mechanisms: Local atomic pair interactions (especially Al–Ni and Al–Co) drive clustering and ordering within the high-temperature BCC matrix.
Competing thermodynamic instabilities (negative mixing enthalpies for certain pairs vs. positive ones for others) set an energetic landscape that dictates phase separation.
Kinetic factors, including cooling rate and deformation-induced defects, facilitate diffusionless martensitic transformations and cellular precipitation.
disagreements: There is some variation over the exact temperature ranges and conditions at which transitions (e.g., BCC to B2 vs. BCC to FCC) occur; simulations sometimes predict sharper transitions than seen experimentally.
The relative importance of kinetic sluggish diffusion versus thermodynamic driving forces in relieving instability remains debated.
Some studies emphasize clustering mechanisms while others point to diffusionless martensitic transformations, highlighting differences in interpreting phase stability.
open_questions: How can the interplay between thermodynamic instability (as determined by composition-dependent mixing enthalpies) and kinetic constraints (e.g., cooling rate, strain) be quantitatively connected to predict phase stability across the full thermal regime?
Is there a universal, single mechanistic pathway that governs the transformation from the high-temperature BCC state to lower-temperature ordered or phase-separated states in these alloys?
What is the precise role of specific elemental pair correlations (e.g., Al–Ni vs. Al–Co) in determining both the nucleation and growth of secondary phases?
opportunities: Design controlled experiments on Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 where high-temperature BCC samples are subjected to systematically varied cooling rates and controlled deformation to test the kinetics of ordering versus phase separation.
Combine atomistic simulations (with refined interatomic potentials) with in situ high-temperature microscopy to directly observe predicted clustering and ordering transitions.

Explore perturbations (e.g., slight compositional variations or introduction of defects) as baseline comparisons to distinguish the contributions of thermodynamics versus kinetics, with the boundary condition being the maintenance of a high-temperature BCC state.

Develop a hybrid predictive model that integrates first-principles thermodynamic calculations with kinetic Monte Carlo or phase-field methods to link elemental interactions to the experimentally observed phase stability.

directions.type: Composition design and mechanism study via simulation and diffraction
directions.assessment: Directly targets the hypothesis that strong, composition‐dependent pair interactions (e.g., Al–Ni and Al–Co) govern the ordering transition from the high‐temperature BCC state. Simulations and diffraction work from earlier studies support this possibility (e.g. PMC4976365::web::012::summary, PMC6207727::web::017::temperature_dependent_ordering_within_th). This approach is feasible with current computational tools and in situ diffraction experiments.

By systematically varying cooling rates from the high-temperature BCC state, one can decouple the thermodynamic driving force (from composition‐dependent mixing energies) from kinetic arrest. Prior evidence (PMC5043342::web::000::abstract, PMC5043342::web::011::kinetic_effect_and_tailoring_phases_in_c) supports the role of kinetics and makes this an informative and relatively straightforward experimental route.

Using first-principles derived interaction parameters integrated with kinetic Monte Carlo or phase-field models can quantitatively predict the transformation temperature and phase boundaries. The literature (PMC6207727::web::006::monte_carlo_model_for_multi_component_tr, PMC6207727::web::003::introduction) supports such hybrid predictive approaches. This avenue would provide a predictive, composition‐dependent explanation that bridges thermodynamics and kinetics.

Real-time observation (e.g., in situ TEM or synchrotron XRD) of the evolution of ordered domains within the high-temperature BCC matrix would allow direct correlation of local clustering events with macroscopic phase transformation events. The approach is challenging but feasible and builds upon prior work (e.g. PMC7282864::web::023::discussion) to visualize diffusionless ordering.

Applying controlled strain has been shown to promote clustering-to-ordering transitions in similar systems (e.g. PMC4976365::web::012::summary). Although it provides an alternate pathway to test kinetic sensitivity, it is more complex and less directly linked to the thermal evolution governed by composition‐dependent thermodynamic instability.
